title: The Weight of Light: Colliding Pulses of Radiation in General Relativity
hook: General Relativity predicts pure light alone can collapse into a black hole — and colliding two such pulses head-on can yield one big black hole, two small ones, or none at all.
key_points: Light carries energy, and energy curves spacetime — so pure radiation can collapse into a black hole.
This paper numerically simulates light pulses right up to and beyond the collapse threshold.
Near collapse, pulses reach a 'compactness' beyond what the hoop conjecture predicts for ordinary matter.
A single strong-enough pulse collapses directly into a fast-moving black hole.
Colliding two pulses head-on can yield two small black holes, one big one, or none — depending on tuning.
content_html: A new arXiv paper by Jorge Expósito Patiño, Vitor Cardoso, and Hannes R. Rüter takes one of General Relativity's strangest implications seriously: light itself carries energy, and energy curves spacetime, so squeezing enough pure radiation into a small enough space should make it collapse into a black hole — no matter required at all. The team numerically simulates strong pulses of electromagnetic radiation right up to, and beyond, that collapse threshold.
extra_html: Near the threshold, the pulses reach a compactness that exceeds the maximum the "hoop conjecture" predicts should be possible for ordinary matter. Push a single pulse past the threshold and it collapses straight into a fast-moving black hole. Collide two pulses head-on, and depending on how precisely they're tuned, the outcome can be two horizonless remnants, two small black holes, or one single large black hole — showing that light colliding with light alone can carve out genuinely new states of spacetime.

related.title: Black Holes
related.hook: A black hole is a place where gravity wins so completely that nothing — not even light — can escape once it crosses the edge called the event horizon.

related.title: E = mc²: Mass Is Energy
related.hook: The most famous equation in physics says mass and energy are the same thing. Because the speed of light squared is a colossal number, a tiny bit of mass holds a staggering amount of energy.

flashcards.prompt: Why does General Relativity predict that pure light alone could collapse into a black hole?
flashcards.back_html: Light carries energy, and energy curves spacetime — so squeezing enough radiation into a small enough region can make it collapse under its own gravity.

flashcards.prompt: What happens when a single pulse of light is pushed past the collapse threshold?

choices.text: It collapses directly into a fast-moving black hole
It settles into an ordinary star

flashcards.explanation_html: Above the threshold, a single pulse of radiation collapses straight into a fast-moving black hole, per the paper's simulations.

flashcards.prompt: What can happen when two strong light pulses collide head-on, depending on tuning?

choices.text: Two horizonless remnants, two small black holes, or one big black hole
Always exactly one medium-sized black hole
The pulses always cancel out and vanish

flashcards.explanation_html: Depending on precise tuning, the collision yields two horizonless states, two small black holes, or one single large black hole.

flashcards.prompt: How compact do the pulses get near the collapse threshold?
flashcards.back_html: Compact enough to exceed the maximum "compactness" the hoop conjecture predicts should be possible for ordinary matter.
